newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: OPINION - CZECH NATO MEMBERSHIP, BY JIRI PEHE.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - CZECH NATO MEMBERSHIP, BY JIRI PEHE.

text.p: Research Director, Open Media Research Institute

PRAGUE, March 5 - The July NATO summit -- to decide which East European countries will be offered membership in the first wave and the recent proposal by U.S. Secretary of State Madeliene Albright to speed up NATO expansion -- has set off a heated debate in the Czech Republic.
A number of politicians and political commentators suggest the Czech Army is not ready to join NATO.

Various opinion polls show that less than half of the population support their country's membership in NATO. The opposition Social Democrats (CSSD) suggest membership should be decided in a referendum.
All three parties in the ruling coalition are staunchly opposed to a referendum.

Almost immediately after CSSD Chairman Milos Zeman announced at the end of February that his party is in favor of a referendum on NATO membership, Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec accused the Social Democrats of planning to drag the country into a counterproductive political battle similar to a recent one surrounding the approval of the Czech-German Declaration in the lower chamber of the parliament.
Zieleniec charged that in proposing a referendum, the CSSD again wants to court extreme-right and extreme-left voters.

True, should the CSSD insist on a referendum, one of the most important steps in the country's modern history -- that NATO membership undoubtedly represents -- could fall victim to political passions far exceeding those witnessed during the debate surrounding the Czech-German declaration.

Both ultra-right Republicans and unreformed Communists are staunchly opposed to NATO membership. Any further integration into Western structures represents a major defeat for the two parties, both of which thrive on xenophobia and instability.

At the same time, Zieleniec's attack on the CSSD was partly unjust. A referendum on NATO membership is not a new CSSD strategy aimed at courting extremists; the party called for a referendum already in its electoral platform last spring.
Zeman could propose dropping the referendum idea from the platform. But his insisting on a referendum can also be seen as an honest effort to live up to promises given to CSSD voters.
A referendum represents a nightmare for coalition politicians mainly because they have not managed to convince a majority of Czechs that NATO membership is necessary.

While Czech politicians have been very active internationally in trying to persuade Western countries that NATO should be expanded and that the Czech Republic should be among the first countries to be admitted, they have failed to run an effective campaign at home.
As a result, most Czechs do not seem to know what NATO membership is good for or why they should care at all.

The situation is very different from that in Poland, where security issues are high on politicians' agenda. Opinion polls show a majority of Poles still fear Russia and see their country's security as better protected if Poland joins NATO.
Most Czechs, on the other hand, do not see Russia as a threat; the symbolic value of NATO membership has played a larger role than security concerns.

But just like in Hungary, the importance of symbolism attached to NATO membership has diminished as NATO has procrastinated with its expansion and as, at the same time, the country has become a member of other Western organizations.

The Czechs have a long anti-militaristic tradition. Unlike in Poland, the Czech army is not held in high regard. And neither the army nor the government has done enough to convince people that the army really matters--quite to the contrary.
The government has repeatedly failed to provide the army with a large enough budget to be able to modernize and adjust rapidly to Western standards.
Strategies to modernize the army, submitted by various defense ministers, have been rejected by the government; and currently no such comprehensive strategy exists.

Army officials admit that the army has not done enough to adjust to Western standards. An open competition for supplying a command communication system compatible with those used by NATO has been bogged down in a bureaucratic maze.
The army also could not find recently 100 of 700 documents which NATO started giving to Partnership for Peace countries in 1994 in an effort to prepare them for possible full membership.

Given the low level of support for NATO membership among Czechs, one can argue that should NATO membership be approved only by the parliament, it may be challenged by extremist as not representative of the public's feelings for years to come. Holding a referendum would represent a way out.

On the other hand, a referendum would stir up an emotional and possibly destabilizing debate that the country--still recovering from the political farce surrounding the adoption of the Czech-German Declaration-- can ill afford.
Moreover, the coalition rightly argues that unlike membership in the European Union, NATO membership does not amount to giving up parts of national sovereignty.
The CSSD supports NATO membership--though it is opposed to stationing foreign troops and placing nuclear weapons on the country's territory.
Some CSSD deputies have indicated they do not support holding a referendum. The CSSD may therefore consider dropping the idea of a referendum at its upcoming congress.
In the meantime, coalition politicians are doing their best to play down low support for membership. Some are even using arguments bordering on demagoguery.

For example, Foreign Minister Zieleniec went as far as recently arguing that an opinion poll by his ministry, which showed that a majority of people think NATO membership would increase the country's security, indicated that a majority of Czechs were in favor of NATO membership.
It, of course, did not.
(Note - the opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters.)
